title: The daemon gets its first durable recurring schedule, restart-safe and never doubled
description:
SPIDR grandchild A of task-6ec875f4dd5f4f2ab97e46f71bf57b2b (architect-aa54e231, 2026-09-05), split because the parent needed the daemon's FIRST recurring loop plus a probe, a bounded ring, a derived state and an incident - five pieces over twelve-plus files. This row is the dependency-free LEAF and it is pure infrastructure. Grandchild B consumes it.

THE DAEMON HAS NO RECURRING LOOP AT ALL. Measured at HEAD (branch moe/work-2026-09-04): `grep -rn "setInterval" apps/daemon/src --include=*.ts` excluding tests returns ZERO, and daemon-main.ts has no periodic tick. Everything the daemon does today is request-driven or spawn-driven. So this row is not "add a timer to the existing scheduler" - it is the first scheduled work in the process, and that is exactly why the parent's DoD 3 hazard exists.

WHAT THIS ROW OWNS: a durable recurring schedule. Registered targets with a per-target interval, persisted so a restart resumes them, and an IDEMPOTENT registration so a restart cannot end up running the same target twice.

THE DOUBLE SCHEDULE IS THE SUBJECT. A restart that re-registers an already-scheduled target doubles the rate SILENTLY - the symptom is a durable store filling twice as fast, never an error, and nobody looks until the store is large. Assert the RATE across a restart, not merely that work resumed. A test that only checks "it is still scheduled" passes for a doubled schedule.

BUILD IT INJECTABLE. Take the clock and the timer as ports the way `verifier-process-runner.ts` takes `spawn`, `timeoutMs`, `killGraceMs` and `killProcessGroup` (options at :45-56) - a scheduler tested against a real wall clock is slow and flaky, and this repo already has a spawn-latency cliff that reds timing-sensitive tests (~10 s stalls). Every arm here must run on a fake clock in milliseconds.

STOP CLEANLY. Timers keep a node process alive; a schedule with no shutdown path makes the daemon unkillable and makes every test that starts one leak a handle. Copy `verifier-process-runner.ts`'s discipline: one cleanup, called on every exit path, idempotent (:107-118).

NOT IN SCOPE: the health probe itself, the probe ring, UP/DEGRADED/DOWN, and the incident - all grandchild B. No UI.

VERIFY: `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test`.
definitionOfDone: A target registered with an interval runs on that interval, asserted on an INJECTED clock and timer rather than a real one - no arm in this row may depend on wall-clock time, because the measured spawn-latency cliff on this host reds timing-sensitive tests for unrelated reasons.

REGISTRATION IS IDEMPOTENT: registering the same target twice leaves ONE schedule, asserted by counting executions over a fixed window rather than by inspecting a registry. A registry-count assertion passes for a design that stores one entry and arms two timers.

SURVIVES A RESTART WITH NO DOUBLE SCHEDULE: rebuild the scheduler from durable records and assert the post-restart execution RATE equals the pre-restart rate over the same window. Asserting that work merely resumed is what lets a silently doubled schedule ship - and its only symptom is a store filling twice as fast.

EVERY TIMER IS RELEASED ON SHUTDOWN, asserted by the process being able to exit (or by an explicit handle count), not by a flag. A leaked interval keeps node alive and makes any test that starts a schedule leak into its neighbours.
The per-target interval is durable and a target with no interval takes a stated default; assert the default is applied rather than the target being skipped.
Gates quoted with their `Test Files N passed` count lines: `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test`, `pnpm typecheck`.
taskRails: NO DOUBLE SCHEDULE, AND ASSERT THE RATE. 'It resumed after restart' is the assertion that lets a doubled schedule through; only counting executions over a window catches it.
INJECTED CLOCK AND TIMER ONLY. No arm may wait on real time: this host has a measured spawn-latency cliff that reds timing-sensitive tests for reasons unrelated to the code.
ONE CLEANUP, ON EVERY EXIT PATH, IDEMPOTENT - copy verifier-process-runner.ts:107-118. A leaked interval keeps the process alive and contaminates neighbouring tests.
THIS IS THE DAEMON'S FIRST SCHEDULED WORK. Keep it generic and free of health-probe vocabulary: grandchild B is its first consumer, not its owner.
NO PROBE, NO RING, NO INCIDENT, NO UI - grandchild B and the parent's children 2 and 3.

implementationPlan.description:
MEASURE AT CLAIM. This row is dependency-free, so there is nothing to wait on — but re-measure the two facts it rests on.

  (a) `grep -rn 'setInterval' apps/daemon/src --include=*.ts | grep -v '\.test\.'` — at plan time (2026-09-05, branch moe/work-2026-09-04) this returned ZERO. If a recurring loop has appeared since, STOP and report: someone else built the daemon's first scheduler and this row would be a silent duplicate. Read `git log -- <that file>` to find the owner.
  (b) `grep -n 'shutdown\|SIGINT\|SIGTERM' apps/daemon/src/daemon-main.ts` — the shutdown chain this row hooks into. Measured: `daemon-main.ts` is 235 lines with `shutdownWithOperator` at :201, `started.shutdown()` at :205, and SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers at :228-232 that call `shutdown(trigger)` then `process.exit(0)`. That chain is where DoD 4's timer release belongs — not a new signal handler of your own, which would race the existing one.

There is NO settings directory in the daemon (`ls apps/daemon/src/settings` — absent), so durable records go in the EVENT STORE. Copy the commit shape from `apps/daemon/src/environment/environment-store.ts:91-115` — aggregate id helper, `commandBytes` carrying the subject only, `commandId ?? randomUUID()`, `committedAt: config.now()`, one event with a JSON payload, `expectedVersion: store.getAggregateVersion(aggregateId)` — and fold on read the way `environment-projection.ts:80-87` does. The `@moe/store` dependency edge is already proven: apps/daemon/package.json:31 declares it and environment-projection.ts:1 imports the bare specifier and typechecks today.

Read `apps/daemon/src/orchestrator/verifier-process-runner.ts` before writing any lifecycle: injectable `spawn`/`timeoutMs`/`killGraceMs`/`killProcessGroup` options (:45-56), and ONE idempotent `cleanup()` clearing every timer, called on every exit path (:107-118). That is the shape to copy.

RED TESTS FIRST, ALL ON A FAKE CLOCK. Write these and watch them fail. Rail 2 is absolute: no arm in this row may wait on wall-clock time. This host has a measured spawn-latency cliff (~10 s stalls) that reds timing-sensitive tests for reasons unrelated to the code, so a scheduler asserted against real time would be both slow and flaky, and its failures would be unattributable.

Inject BOTH the clock and the timer. The test drives time forward explicitly and counts executions; nothing sleeps.

  1. INTERVAL IS HONOURED (DoD 1). A target registered at interval N executes once per N of injected time. Advance a known window and assert the exact execution COUNT, not merely that it ran at least once.
  2. REGISTRATION IS IDEMPOTENT (DoD 2). Register the SAME target twice, advance a fixed window, assert the execution count equals the single-registration count. Assert by COUNTING EXECUTIONS, never by inspecting a registry: a design that stores one entry while arming two timers passes a registry-count assertion and is exactly the bug.
  3. RESTART DOES NOT DOUBLE (DoD 3). Run a window, record the rate. Rebuild the scheduler from its durable records the way a restart would, run the SAME window again, and assert the second rate EQUALS the first. "It resumed" is the assertion that lets a doubled schedule ship, and a doubled schedule's only symptom is a durable store filling twice as fast — never an error.
  4. THE DEFAULT INTERVAL APPLIES (DoD 5). A target registered with no interval runs at the stated default — assert it EXECUTES at that rate, not that it was skipped. A scheduler that silently skips an interval-less target looks identical to one with nothing registered.
  5. SHUTDOWN RELEASES (DoD 4). After shutdown, advancing the clock produces NO further executions, and a second shutdown is harmless.

Assert against the production surface; do not write a helper that re-derives tick counts.

THE SCHEDULER CORE — a new focused module under apps/daemon/src/orchestrator/ plus its one-line `.js` bridge (copy the shape of `environment-store.js`).

KEEP IT GENERIC (rail 4). This is the daemon's first scheduled work and grandchild B is its FIRST CONSUMER, not its owner. No health-probe vocabulary anywhere in it — no `probe`, no `environment`, no `healthUrl`. A target is an id, an interval and a callback. The next consumer should not need a second scheduler.

Ports, all injectable, following verifier-process-runner.ts's option shape:
  - `now(): number` and the timer pair (set/clear), so every arm runs on a fake clock;
  - the store, for the durable half in step 4.

IDEMPOTENT REGISTRATION IS THE CORE INVARIANT. Registering a target id that is already scheduled must leave exactly ONE armed timer — replace or no-op, decide deliberately and say which in the step note. Guard it in ONE place: if the in-memory arm and the durable write can disagree about whether a target is already scheduled, the double-schedule returns by that seam.

A TARGET THAT THROWS MUST NOT KILL THE SCHEDULE. Wrap each execution so a failing callback is contained and the next tick still fires — a probe that throws once should not silently stop all monitoring. Decide whether a repeatedly-throwing target is retried forever or backed off, and say which; do not leave it undefined.

AND EXECUTIONS MUST NOT OVERLAP: if a target's callback is still running when its next tick arrives, skip rather than stack. A slow HTTP probe on a 60 s interval that takes 90 s would otherwise accumulate concurrent runs and fill the store faster than its stated rate — the same symptom as a doubled schedule, from a different cause.

Keep the module under 250 lines.

THE DURABLE HALF — persistence and the restart rebuild.

Persist each registered target (id, interval, and whatever a consumer needs to reconstruct its callback binding) in the EVENT STORE, using the `environment-store.ts:91-115` commit shape named in step 1. Fold on read to get the current target set, the way `environment-projection.ts:80-87` does — later events win, and a malformed record DROPS the target rather than being ignored, matching `environment-fold.ts:12-16`'s reasoning: silently resurrecting a stale target is the more dangerous reading, because a dropped target is visibly absent while a resurrected one runs at an interval nobody chose.

THE REBUILD IS WHERE THE DOUBLE SCHEDULE HAPPENS. On start, the scheduler reads its durable targets and arms them. The hazard is a start path that arms from durable records AND a caller that also re-registers the same targets — each is individually correct and together they double the rate. Make registration idempotent ACROSS the rebuild, not just within a single process: the durable record is the identity, so re-registering a target that the rebuild already armed must be a no-op, and step 2's arm 3 is what proves it.

A target's callback cannot be persisted. Decide how a rebuilt target reacquires its behaviour — a consumer-supplied resolver keyed by target id is the obvious shape — and state it; an unresolvable target after restart must be a visible refusal or a dropped target, never a silently armed timer with no work attached.

SHUTDOWN AND COMPOSITION — the only edit to an existing file in this row.

ONE IDEMPOTENT CLEANUP that clears every armed timer, in the shape of `verifier-process-runner.ts:107-118`. Calling it twice is harmless; calling it while a target is mid-execution does not throw.

HOOK IT INTO THE EXISTING SHUTDOWN CHAIN in `apps/daemon/src/daemon-main.ts`, NOT a new signal handler. Measured: `shutdownWithOperator` at :201 awaits `started.shutdown()` at :205, and the SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers at :228-232 call `shutdown(trigger)` then `process.exit(0)`. Add your release to that existing chain — registering your own `process.once("SIGINT", …)` would race the handler already there and could exit before the release runs. daemon-main.ts is 235 lines; add as little as the wiring needs.

WHY THE RELEASE MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS: an armed interval keeps the node event loop alive, so a scheduler with no release makes the daemon unkillable by its own shutdown path — and makes every test that starts one leak a handle into its neighbours, which on this suite surfaces as unrelated timeouts. If you use `unref()` so the timer never holds the loop open, that is a reasonable belt-and-braces choice but it is NOT a substitute for the release: an unref'd timer still fires while the process lives, so a shutdown that only unrefs keeps probing after the daemon believes it stopped. State which you did and why.

DoD 4 asks for the assertion to be the process being able to exit, or an explicit handle count — NOT a flag. A boolean proves only that the code believed it released.

GATES AND DRILLS.

GATES, each STANDALONE and FOREGROUND — no pipe, no `;` chain, no `&&` (a piped run reports tail's exit code; a chain reports only the last command's):
  1. `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test`
  2. `pnpm typecheck`
READ THE OUTPUT, NOT THE EXIT CODE: a missed `--filter` exits 0, and "No test files found" / "0 passed" are also exit 0. The discriminator is `Test Files N passed` with N nonzero — quote it for both. A bare `pnpm test` covers no `apps/**` and is not evidence. Name `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test` as the complete_task verification command.

The daemon suite is slow (~22 min) and flaky on this branch (two back-to-back baselines gave `17 failed | 416 passed` then `10 failed | 423 passed`, dominated by 30000ms timeouts), so attribute red by PATH per global rail 3, never by whole-suite delta. Run your own suite targeted first. WATCH FOR NEW TIMEOUTS IN UNRELATED FILES: that is the signature of a leaked interval from this row contaminating its neighbours, and it is the one red here you should treat as YOURS even though the failing file is not.

DRILL 1, THE SUBJECT OF THE ROW. Make the restart rebuild arm targets WITHOUT the idempotence guard. Step 2's arm 3 MUST go red on the RATE comparison. If it stays green, the arm is asserting that work resumed rather than comparing rates — rewrite it before accepting, because that is exactly the assertion that lets a doubled schedule ship.
DRILL 2, IDEMPOTENCE. Register the same target twice with the guard removed; arm 2 must go red on the execution COUNT. If your arm inspects a registry instead, it will stay green — which is the point of the drill.
DRILL 3, THE RELEASE. Remove the cleanup from the shutdown chain; arm 5 must go red. Confirm it fails on "executions after shutdown", not on a flag.

RESTORE PROOF, global rail 13. `git status --porcelain` the exact mutated paths BEFORE drilling. `daemon-main.ts` is TRACKED, so an empty `git diff -- apps/daemon/src/daemon-main.ts` is valid proof, run in a call SEPARATE from the restore. Your new modules are UNTRACKED and `git diff` is BLIND to them — back each up out of tree (%TEMP%, suffixed with your worker id) before mutating and prove the restore by SHA256 equality against that backup.

COMPLETION RECORD states: that this is the daemon's first recurring loop and the grep proving it was the only one; the idempotence decision (replace vs no-op) and where it is guarded; the overlap policy and the throwing-target policy; how a rebuilt target reacquires its callback and what happens when it cannot; whether `unref` was used and why it is not the release; and the three drill outcomes with restore proofs.

planningNotes.approachesConsidered:
MAKING THE SCHEDULER HEALTH-PROBE-SHAPED — rejected by rail 4 and by simple foresight: grandchild B is its first CONSUMER, not its owner. A scheduler carrying `probe`/`environment`/`healthUrl` vocabulary forces the next consumer to write a second one, and two schedulers in one process is the double-schedule hazard institutionalised.

ASSERTING IDEMPOTENCE BY INSPECTING A REGISTRY — rejected explicitly in the plan and drilled. A design that stores ONE entry while arming TWO timers passes a registry-count assertion and is precisely the bug. Only counting executions over a window distinguishes them.

ASSERTING THE RESTART BY "IT RESUMED" — the assertion that lets a doubled schedule ship. DoD 3 and drill 1 both require a RATE comparison over the same window.

`unref()` AS THE RELEASE — considered and explicitly rejected as a substitute. An unref'd timer does not hold the event loop open, which is a reasonable belt-and-braces choice, but it STILL FIRES while the process lives — so a shutdown that only unrefs keeps probing after the daemon believes it stopped. The plan allows unref alongside a real release and requires the worker to say which they did.

A NEW SIGNAL HANDLER — rejected: it would race the handler already at daemon-main.ts:228-232 and could lose to its `process.exit(0)`.

LEAVING OVERLAP AND THROWING-TARGET BEHAVIOUR UNDEFINED — rejected. Both are decisions a scheduler must make and both produce the same symptom as the bug this row exists to prevent: a callback slower than its interval stacks concurrent runs and fills the store faster than the stated rate, and an unhandled throw silently stops all monitoring. The plan requires each to be decided and stated.

So there is no scheduler to extend and no prior art in-repo for the restart hazard; that is why this was carved out as the dependency-free leaf of task-6ec875f4 rather than left inside it.

THE SHUTDOWN CHAIN TO HOOK, measured: daemon-main.ts is 235 lines. `shutdownWithOperator` at :201 awaits `started.shutdown()` at :205; the SIGINT/SIGTERM handlers at :228-232 call `shutdown(trigger)` then `process.exit(0)`. NO SETTINGS DIRECTORY EXISTS (`ls apps/daemon/src/settings` — absent), so durable target records go in the EVENT STORE. The commit shape to copy is `environment-store.ts:91-115` (aggregate id helper, commandBytes carrying the subject only, `commandId ?? randomUUID()`, `committedAt: config.now()`, one JSON-payload event, `expectedVersion: store.getAggregateVersion(aggregateId)`), folding on read as `environment-projection.ts:80-87` does. THE FOLD'S DROP-ON-MALFORMED DISCIPLINE TRANSFERS, and its reasoning is stronger here than where it came from: `environment-fold.ts:12-16` drops a variable rather than ignoring a corrupt record, because silently resurrecting the previous value is the more dangerous reading. For a scheduler, a resurrected target runs at an interval nobody chose, while a dropped target is visibly absent.

THE LIFECYCLE SHAPE TO COPY: `verifier-process-runner.ts` takes `spawn`, `timeoutMs`, `killGraceMs` and `killProcessGroup` as injectable options (:45-56) and has ONE idempotent `cleanup()` clearing every timer on every exit path (:107-118). A scheduler needs exactly that plus an injected clock.

WHY EVERY ARM MUST RUN ON A FAKE CLOCK: this host has a measured spawn-latency cliff (~10 s stalls) that reds timing-sensitive tests for reasons unrelated to the code under test, and the daemon suite is already flaky with 30000ms timeouts dominating its failures. A scheduler asserted against wall-clock time would be slow, flaky, and its failures unattributable — so the clock and the timer are both ports.
planningNotes.risks:
1. THE DOUBLE SCHEDULE ACROSS THE REBUILD SEAM. The start path arms from durable records AND the caller re-registers the same targets; each is individually correct and together they double the rate. Idempotence must hold ACROSS the rebuild, keyed on the durable identity, not just within one process. This is the row's whole subject and drill 1 targets it.

2. AN IDEMPOTENCE ARM THAT INSPECTS A REGISTRY. Passes for one entry with two armed timers. Must count executions.

3. A LEAKED INTERVAL CONTAMINATING NEIGHBOURS. An armed timer keeps the event loop alive: the daemon becomes unkillable by its own shutdown path, and every test that starts a schedule leaks a handle. On this suite that surfaces as timeouts in UNRELATED files — a red the worker should treat as theirs even though the failing file is not.

4. OVERLAPPING EXECUTIONS. A 90 s callback on a 60 s interval stacks concurrent runs and fills the store faster than the stated rate — indistinguishable in symptom from a doubled schedule, and arriving from a different cause, so a fix aimed at registration would not touch it.

5. A THROWING TARGET KILLING THE SCHEDULE. One failing probe silently ending all monitoring is the worst failure mode available to a monitoring feature, and the natural implementation (an unwrapped callback in a tick) produces it.

6. A REBUILT TARGET WITH NO CALLBACK. Callbacks cannot be persisted; an unresolvable target after restart must refuse or drop visibly, never arm a timer with no work attached — which would look healthy and do nothing.

7. TIMING-SENSITIVE ARMS on a host with a measured spawn-latency cliff would be flaky and unattributable. Fake clock throughout, per rail 2.

8. A SECOND SCHEDULER APPEARING FIRST. Step 1 re-greps for setInterval: if someone else landed one since plan time, this row is a duplicate and must stop rather than add a rival.
